---
title: "08 — Transforms on Subsets and Divisors"
---

## The same trick, on a different index set

In [Chapter 06](../06-polynomials/chapter.qmd) a quadratic-looking sum
$c_k = \sum_{i+j=k}a_ib_j$ became pointwise multiplication after evaluating at
roots of unity. Contests ask the same question with the addition replaced by
something else:

$$h[S] = \sum_{A \cup B = S}f[A]\,g[B], \qquad
h[s] = \sum_{a \oplus b = s}f[a]\,g[b], \qquad
h[x] = \sum_{\operatorname{lcm}(a,b) = x}f[a]\,g[b].$$

Each of these has a change of coordinates that turns it into
"multiply entry by entry", and each transform is a handful of lines of code.
So the coding is never the hard part. **The hard part is deciding which
relation among indices the statement actually combines** — union, disjoint
union, intersection, XOR, lcm, gcd — because the transforms look almost
identical and none of them will complain if you pick the wrong one.

That is the skill this chapter builds: read the index relation off the
statement, derive the matching transform, and prove the inverse exists in your
coefficient ring.

Unless stated otherwise, array values live in a commutative ring. The
zeta/Möbius stages use only addition and subtraction; a convolution
additionally needs the pointwise products to make sense.

## Prerequisites, notation, and learning objectives

Read [sets and induction](../00-foundations/chapter.qmd),
[divisor sums](../02-multiplicative-number-theory/chapter.qmd), and
[modular units](../01-modular-algebra/chapter.qmd).

You should finish able to derive a transform from an index relation, prove its
inverse, tell union apart from disjoint union, and choose the correct stage
order for divisor transforms.

The universe is $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, subsets are masks $0,\ldots,2^n-1$, and
$|S|$ is the popcount. A **poset** is a set with a reflexive, antisymmetric,
transitive order; subset inclusion and divisibility are the two we use. A
**zeta transform** sums over predecessors in that order, and a **Möbius
transform** undoes it. Complexities count ring operations, not bit costs for
huge integers.

## 1. Subset zeta and Möbius transforms

The subset zeta transform changes coordinates from "exactly $T$" to "any
subset of $S$":

$$F[S] = \sum_{T \subseteq S}f[T].$$

Read it concretely: if $f[T]$ counts objects whose feature set is exactly $T$,
then $F[S]$ counts objects using *only* features from $S$ — the quantity you
can actually compute by a DP, whereas "exactly" is the quantity you want.

The computation processes one bit at a time: for each bit $b$, add the value
at the mask without $b$ into the mask with $b$. Invert by subtracting in the
same schedule.

*Why this works* is the invariant, not the loop shape. After a set $B$ of bits
has been processed, the value at $S$ is

$$\sum_{\substack{T \subseteq S\\ S\setminus T \subseteq B}}f[T],$$

i.e. only processed bits may have been deleted. Processing one more bit splits
the allowed terms into two disjoint cases — that bit deleted or not — which is
exactly the update.

::: {.callout-note title="Two bits, by hand"}
With $f[\varnothing], f[\{0\}], f[\{1\}], f[\{0,1\}] = (1,2,3,4)$: processing
bit $0$ gives $(1,3,3,7)$, then bit $1$ gives $(1,3,4,10)$. Check the last
entry: $1+2+3+4 = 10$. ✓ Subtracting in the same order restores $(1,2,3,4)$.
:::

Both directions cost $O(n2^n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra memory. The inverse is
legitimate because the Möbius function of the Boolean lattice is
$\mu(T,S) = (-1)^{|S\setminus T|}$; concretely, each butterfly
$(a,b)\mapsto(a,a+b)$ is inverted by $(a,b)\mapsto(a,b-a)$. Bit order does not
matter — the stages commute — but **which member of each pair receives the
update does**: flip it and you have computed a different transform.

The **superset** variants reverse the condition: for masks `s` without bit
`b`, do `f[s] += f[s | (1<<b)]`. Recognition signals: "sum over all
submasks/supermasks", compatibility masks, inclusion–exclusion over missing
features.

### OR and AND convolution

For $h[S] = \sum_{A\cup B=S}f[A]g[B]$: subset-zeta both arrays, multiply
pointwise, subset-Möbius the result. The reason is visible at a fixed $S$,
where the product is

$$\left(\sum_{A\subseteq S}f[A]\right)\left(\sum_{B\subseteq S}g[B]\right),$$

which counts every pair whose union is **contained in** $S$. That is exactly a
zeta transform of the answer, so Möbius inversion turns "contained in" back
into "equal to". For $A \cap B = S$, run the same argument with superset zeta.
Both cost $O(n2^n)$.

## 2. XOR convolution and the Walsh–Hadamard transform

XOR makes masks into the group $(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^n$, where every element
is its own inverse. Groups like this have **characters**: functions turning
the group operation into multiplication. Here they are the sign functions

$$\chi_k(x) = (-1)^{\langle k,x\rangle}, \qquad
\langle k,x\rangle = \textstyle\sum_b k_bx_b \bmod 2,$$

the parity of shared set bits. Since bit parities add,
$\chi_k(a\oplus b) = \chi_k(a)\chi_k(b)$ — and that single identity is the
whole method. Defining $\widehat f[k] = \sum_x f[x]\chi_k(x)$,

$$\widehat h[k] = \sum_{a,b}f[a]g[b]\chi_k(a\oplus b)
= \widehat f[k]\,\widehat g[k]$$

for $h[s] = \sum_{a\oplus b = s}f[a]g[b]$. Convolution becomes pointwise
multiplication in character coordinates.

*Inversion.* Consider $\sum_k \chi_k(x)\chi_k(y)$. If $x = y$ all $2^n$ terms
are $1$. If $x \ne y$, take a bit where they differ and pair each $k$ with the
mask toggling that bit: the two terms have opposite signs and cancel. So
applying the transform twice returns $2^n f$. Splitting the frequency masks by
one bit gives the butterfly $(a,b)\mapsto(a+b,\,a-b)$, and $n$ stages cost
$O(n2^n)$.

::: {.callout-warning title="The $2^n$ must be invertible"}
Inversion divides by $N = 2^n$, so the ring must make $N$ a unit — over a
field, characteristic $\ne 2$. Under an odd prime modulus multiply by
$N^{-1}$; over the integers, transform in a wide type and divide exactly at
the end (intermediate values can be far larger than the final coefficients).

In characteristic two the length-two transform maps both $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$
to $(1,1)$: information is destroyed and no scaling can recover it. OR/AND
transforms use triangular butterflies and need no normalization at all.
:::

**Worked check.** $f = [1,2]$, $g = [3,4]$. Directly,
$h = [1\cdot3+2\cdot4,\ 1\cdot4+2\cdot3] = [11,10]$. By transform:
$\widehat f = [3,-1]$, $\widehat g = [7,-1]$, product $[21,1]$, and the
inverse butterfly gives $[(21+1)/2,\ (21-1)/2] = [11,10]$. ✓

## 3. Subset convolution: when the parts must be disjoint

The disjoint-union convolution

$$h[S] = \sum_{T\subseteq S}f[T]\,g[S\setminus T]$$

is the one that appears in "partition this set into two labelled parts" DPs.
Direct enumeration over submasks costs $O(3^n)$. The trick to reach
$O(n^22^n)$ is to **carry the set size as an extra index**, because
disjointness is a statement about sizes:

$$|A| + |B| = |A\cup B| + |A\cap B|,$$

so among pairs with $A\cup B = S$, the disjoint ones are exactly those with
$|A|+|B| = |S|$.

So: split each array by rank ($f_k[S] = f[S]$ when $|S| = k$, else $0$), zeta
each rank, form

$$H_k[S] = \sum_{i=0}^{k}F_i[S]\,G_{k-i}[S],$$

Möbius each rank back, and read off $h[S] = H_{|S|}[S]$. After inversion,
rank $k$ at mask $S$ holds pairs with $A\cup B = S$ and $|A|+|B| = k$;
selecting $k = |S|$ keeps precisely the disjoint ones. Time $O(n^22^n)$,
memory $O(n2^n)$.

::: {.callout-warning title="Do not prune overlapping ranks early"}
It is tempting to zero out entries with $k > |S|$ before inversion. Don't:
those entries hold overlapping pairs that must still **cancel** at larger
masks. Two copies of the singleton $\{0\}$ produce a rank-two contribution at
mask $\{0\}$ *and*, after zeta, at $\{0,1\}$; inversion subtracts one from the
other. Deleting the first leaves a phantom disjoint pair at $\{0,1\}$.
:::

For $S = \{0,1\}$ the wanted sum is

$$f[\varnothing]g[S] + f[\{0\}]g[\{1\}] + f[\{1\}]g[\{0\}] + f[S]g[\varnothing],$$

whereas OR convolution would also admit overlapping pairs such as $(S,S)$.
The rank index is the only thing separating them.

Use it when a transition splits a set into two labelled disjoint parts and
$n \approx 20$. If one side is sparse, plain $O(3^n)$ submask enumeration can
be both faster and easier.

**Budget the memory before you code it.** At $n = 20$, one ranked array of
32-bit entries takes $21\cdot 2^{20}\cdot 4 \approx 84$ MiB; three of them are
252 MiB. Count the arrays that are simultaneously live against the actual
limit — the asymptotic bound alone promises nothing.

## 4. Divisor-poset transforms

Order positive integers by divisibility instead of inclusion and the whole
story repeats, with primes playing the role of bits:

$$F[x] = \sum_{d \mid x}f[d] \quad(\text{divisor zeta}), \qquad
G[x] = \sum_{x \mid m}f[m] \quad(\text{multiple zeta}).$$

For arrays up to $N$, divisor zeta runs one stage per prime $p$, doing
`f[i*p] += f[i]` for $1 \le i \le \lfloor N/p\rfloor$, **ascending** in $i$;
the inverse subtracts **descending**. Multiple zeta uses `f[i] += f[i*p]`
descending, and inverts ascending.

*Why direction matters.* The stage must accumulate along a whole prime-power
chain, then undo it in reverse dependency order. On the chain $1,2,4$ with
values $(a,b,c)$, ascending updates give $(a,\,a+b,\,a+b+c)$ — correct, since
index $4$ must include $f[1]$. Descending updates would give $(a,\,a+b,\,b+c)$,
silently dropping $a$ from index $4$. To invert, subtract index $2$ from index
$4$ first, then index $1$ from index $2$.

The invariant matches the subset case: after processing a set $P$ of primes,
the value at $x$ sums $f[d]$ over divisors $d$ such that every prime factor of
$x/d$ lies in $P$. Each stage adds all choices of one prime's exponent, and
unique factorization is what makes the stages commute.

**Which one for which operation.** For **lcm** convolution, "both operands
divide $x$" is the transformed condition, so use divisor zeta, multiply, and
invert. For **gcd** convolution, the condition is "both operands are multiples
of $x$", so use multiple zeta. Prime-stage transforms cost $O(N\log\log N)$
(versus $O(N\log N)$ for direct divisor loops).

Preconditions: indices start at $1$, and you must decide explicitly what
happens at $0$, since $\gcd(0,x)$ and $\operatorname{lcm}(0,x)$ make it a
special element.

One subtlety about truncation: the lcm output only covers $1,\ldots,N$, and
pairs with lcm above $N$ simply appear nowhere. That is harmless, because for
any retained $x$ both operands divide $x$ and so are themselves in range. For
gcd convolution every pair of in-range inputs has an in-range gcd.

## 5. Pitfalls and decision guide

- `A | B`, `A & B`, and `A ^ B` need three different transforms. Visual
  similarity is not algebraic equivalence.
- Do the Möbius inversion in the same ring as the sums; under a modulus,
  normalize subtractions.
- Subset convolution hits the memory limit before the time limit. Use
  contiguous rank-major storage.
- SOS DP often needs only the forward transform. Don't pay for an inverse you
  never use.
- To decide *which* XOR values are reachable, a linear basis
  ([Chapter 07](../07-linear-algebra/chapter.qmd)) beats FWT. Use FWT when you
  need multiplicities or a distribution over every XOR value.

## 6. Solved exercises

### A. Union is not disjoint union

On a two-element universe let $f[\{0\}] = g[\{0\}] = 1$ and everything else be
zero. Compute the OR convolution and the disjoint-union convolution.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
There is exactly one ordered pair with nonzero weight. Look at its
intersection.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
OR convolution is $1$ at $\{0\}$: the union of the singleton with itself is
itself. Subset convolution is zero everywhere, because the pair overlaps.

In the ranked method that pair carries rank two at a mask of size one, so it
is discarded only at the final step, when rank $|S|$ is selected after
inversion — which is exactly why it must be kept until then.
:::

### B. Count AND-zero subsequences

For the masks $(1,2,3)$ on two bits, count the nonempty subsequences whose AND
is zero. Derive the signs rather than guessing them.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Let $c[S]$ count inputs containing every bit of $S$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In mask order $0,1,2,3$ we get $c = (3,2,2,1)$. A subsequence whose AND
*contains* $S$ is any nonempty subset of those $c[S]$ occurrences, so

$$F[S] = 2^{c[S]} - 1$$

is the **superset zeta** of the exact-AND distribution. Inverting at $S = 0$:
$7 - 3 - 3 + 1 = 2$, namely the subsequences $(1,2)$ and $(1,2,3)$. ✓

In general compute $c$ in $O(n2^n)$ and take
$\sum_S(-1)^{|S|}\bigl(2^{c[S]}-1\bigr)$. Equal input values still count as
distinct occurrences.
:::

### C. Recover exact gcd counts

Both operands are chosen independently from $\{1,2,3,4\}$. How many ordered
pairs have gcd $1, 2, 3, 4$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Pairs with both operands divisible by $d$ number $\lfloor 4/d\rfloor^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $h[d]$ the exact-gcd count, $\lfloor 4/d\rfloor^2 = \sum_{d \mid m}h[m]$.
Subtracting downward from the top: $h[4] = 1$, $h[3] = 1$,
$h[2] = 4 - h[4] = 3$, $h[1] = 16 - 3 - 1 - 1 = 11$. The four values sum to
all $16$ pairs. ✓

This is multiple-zeta inversion. Squaring pointwise counts *ordered*
independent choices; unordered pairs or distinct-index requirements need their
own correction.
:::

## 7. Practice, in order

Labels: **Foundation** isolates one idea; **Advanced** combines it;
**Mastery** requires recognition. All statements are available in English.

1. **Foundation — [Compatible Numbers, CF 165E](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/165/E)**. Superset/subset SOS DP. [Official tutorial](https://codeforces.com/blog/entry/4124).
   - Why: the canonical "find a disjoint present mask" transform.
   <details><summary>Hints</summary>

   1. A number compatible with $x$ is a submask of the complement of $x$.
   2. Store any present witness, then propagate witnesses from submasks.
   3. This uses zeta's dependency order but is not an invertible additive
      transform; no inverse is needed.
   </details>

2. **Advanced — [Jzzhu and Numbers, CF 449D](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/449/D)**. Superset zeta plus inclusion–exclusion. [Official tutorial](https://codeforces.com/blog/entry/13112).
   - Why: converts AND-zero into counts of elements containing each mask (exercise B at full scale).
   <details><summary>Hints</summary>

   1. Count subsequences whose AND contains $S$.
   2. If $c[S]$ inputs contain $S$, there are $2^{c[S]}-1$ nonempty choices.
   3. Möbius-invert, or take the alternating sum by popcount.
   </details>

3. **Advanced — [Nim Counting, AtCoder ABC212 H](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc212/tasks/abc212_h)**. XOR FWT. [Official editorial](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc212/editorial).
   - Why: forces reasoning in character space instead of treating FWT as a black box.
   <details><summary>Hints</summary>

   1. Winning or losing is decided by the XOR of the chosen pile sizes.
   2. Transform the one-choice frequency distribution.
   3. Sum transformed powers for lengths $1$ through $N$, invert, and subtract
      the XOR-zero count. Where the transformed value is $1$, the geometric sum
      is $N$ — do not divide by a vanishing difference.
   </details>

4. **Mastery — [Sum the Fibonacci, CF 914G](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/914/G)**. Ranked subset, XOR, and AND convolutions in one problem. [Official tutorial](https://codeforces.com/blog/entry/57250).
   - Why: the explicit disjointness condition is what turns OR into subset convolution.
   <details><summary>Hints</summary>

   1. Build the frequency array $f$. The pair $(a,b)$ needs $s_a \mathbin\& s_b = 0$,
      so its union distribution is the ranked subset convolution $f * f$.
   2. Get the $(d,e)$ XOR distribution separately, then weight each
      distribution pointwise by the corresponding Fibonacci values.
   3. AND-convolve the three weighted distributions and sum the outputs at
      powers of two. The statement counts ordered five-tuples of indices with
      repetition allowed, so no symmetry division belongs anywhere here.
   </details>

## 8. Reference sheet

| Index relation | Transform | Time | Extra algebra |
|---|---|---|---|
| $A\cup B = S$ | subset zeta / product / inverse | $O(n2^n)$ | ring operations only |
| $A\cap B = S$ | superset zeta / product / inverse | $O(n2^n)$ | ring operations only |
| $A\oplus B = S$ | Walsh–Hadamard | $O(n2^n)$ | $2^n$ a unit, or exact integer division |
| $A\sqcup B = S$ | ranked subset convolution | $O(n^22^n)$ | keep overlap ranks until inversion |
| $\operatorname{lcm}(a,b) = s$ | divisor zeta | $O(N\log\log N)$ | positive indices; output truncated at $N$ |
| $\gcd(a,b) = s$ | multiple zeta | $O(N\log\log N)$ | positive indices |

The recurring proof is always the same: rewrite "exactly this result" as a sum
over "results below (or above) this index", factor the now-independent
choices, and invert. XOR is the exception, using multiplicative signs from
group characters. Decide which proof applies *before* calling the library
routine.
